title: Breaking down large technical initiatives
description: Learn how to take a vague, high-stakes technical project and turn it into clear, executable pieces that a team can deliver incrementally.

data.text: Large technical initiatives often fail not because the team is not smart enough, but because the work was never broken down into pieces small enough to execute, test, and ship. As a senior engineer, one of your most important jobs is to turn a broad goal into a sequence of concrete steps.
Breaking down work is not just about creating tickets. It is about reducing uncertainty, finding the riskiest parts first, and building confidence that the team can actually finish the project.
A common mistake is to start listing tasks before understanding what success looks like. Instead, write down the business outcome first, then work backward to the technical steps needed to reach it.

data.title: Outcome-first decomposition
data.code:
Bad approach:
  - Write migration script
  - Update API
  - Refactor frontend

Good approach:
  Outcome: Customers can save their progress without losing data.
  - Step 1: Add a new column to the database and backfill existing rows.
  - Step 2: Update the API to write to the new column.
  - Step 3: Deploy to staging and run migration tests.
  - Step 4: Roll out to production with a feature flag.
  - Step 5: Remove the old column after validation.

data.text: Not all pieces of a project are equal. Some carry high uncertainty: we do not know if the technology works, if the performance is acceptable, or if the integration will behave as expected. These are the pieces you should tackle first.

items: Build a spike or prototype for the riskiest technology.
Validate assumptions with real data before committing to the full design.
Document the unknowns so the team knows what still needs to be confirmed.
Time-box experiments so they do not turn into unbounded research.

data.text: Each step should deliver value on its own, even if the full project is not complete. That way, the team can ship, learn, and adjust. It also means that if the project is cut short, some value has still been delivered.

data.title: The trunk-based mindset
data.text: If each piece can be merged to main independently, the team moves faster, feedback loops are shorter, and integration headaches disappear. Avoid big-bang merges whenever possible.

data.title: Key takeaways
data.text: Break large initiatives into small, outcome-focused pieces. Tackle the riskiest parts first, validate with real data, and keep each step shippable. This reduces uncertainty and keeps the team moving forward with confidence.
